battle.title: Cache Me If You Can
battle.description: Remember what you computed: memoization, repeated work and call counts.

options: Sorting the inputs so recursion runs faster
Converting recursion into a loop by hand
Using more threads to compute subproblems in parallel
Caching the result of each subproblem the first time it is computed so repeats are looked up
questions.answer: Caching the result of each subproblem the first time it is computed so repeats are looked up
questions.explanation: A memo table stores answers keyed by the subproblem, so overlapping calls cost O(1) after the first. Writing a loop with a table is tabulation, a different (bottom-up) technique.

questions.text: What does this plain recursive Fibonacci program print (the answer, then the number of calls)?
questions.explanation: fib(5) is 5, but plain recursion recomputes the same values: the call count is 15. Counting only 5 calls ignores the repeated subproblems that memoization removes.

questions.text: You must count the paths through a 30 x 30 grid moving only right or down. The plain recursion is far too slow. What is the best fix?
options: Memoize the paths count for each (row, col) cell
Run the same recursion in several threads
Use a bigger int type for the counter
questions.answer: Memoize the paths count for each (row, col) cell
questions.explanation: Paths from a cell depend only on that cell, and many routes reach the same cell, so caching by (row, col) gives 900 states. Threads or a larger type do not remove the repeated work.

questions.text: With a memo table, what is the time complexity of computing fib(n) recursively?
options: O(2^n), the same as plain recursion
O(n), because each value is computed once
O(n^2), because of the memo lookups
questions.answer: O(n), because each value is computed once
questions.explanation: Each of the n states is computed once and then looked up in O(1). Without the memo the same recursion is exponential.

questions.text: This memoized Fibonacci counts every call to fib, including cache hits. For fib(6), what does it print?
questions.explanation: The first descent calls fib(6) down to fib(0): 7 calls. Then fib(3) makes its second call fib(1), and fib(4), fib(5) and fib(6) each make one extra call that hits the cache: 4 more, 11 total. Plain recursion would need 25.

coding.title: Grid Paths With Obstacles
coding.description: A grid has r rows and c columns; each cell is '.' (free) or '#' (blocked). Moving only right or down, count the paths from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell that avoid blocked cells. If the start or end is blocked the answer is 0. Print the count modulo 1000000007.
coding.inputDescription: Line 1: r and c. Then r lines, each a string of c characters ('.' or '#') with no spaces.
coding.outputDescription: A single integer: the number of paths modulo 1000000007.

debug.title: The Forgotten Memo
debug.description: The program reads n and prints the number of ways to climb n stairs taking 1, 2 or 3 steps at a time (n = 0 has 1 way). It uses a memo array but is far too slow: it times out for n around 40 or more. Input: n. Output: the number of ways.
hints: Run it with n = 3, then n = 60. Why does the first answer appear instantly but the second never finishes?
The code reads from memo before computing. Is there any line that ever writes to memo?
The cache is checked but never filled, so every call recomputes the same subproblems exponentially.
Store the computed value with memo[n] = ... before returning it.
